_meta.scope: World overview: era and scale, setting summary, world rules (social/physical constraints of the realistic adaptation), tone and themes, open questions. Faction details belong to politics.json (reference FAC-* only).
_meta.genre_note: Premise (brief.md): 'Realistic fantasy film adapted from a fairy tale' (Lewis Carroll, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland); the fantasy is confined to Alice's dream and rendered photoreal, the waking frame is plain period realism (quote corrected at BIB-0027; the earlier wording 'realistic drama' misquoted brief.md). World rules describe real-world physical and social law; how the source's fantastical elements are reinterpreted is decided in Phase 2 and recorded in cultivation.json.

p2_world_extensions.note: Sections added by p2-world beyond the p0 skeleton, required by the world agent's SOUL (realms / nations, faction presence-and-allegiance register, history overview) and by the work order (real-world frame, realistic counterpart of Wonderland, cross-domain assumptions). They carry no new registered ID prefix: realms and counterparts use plain slug 'key' fields (file-local, never cross-referenced); factions carry 'proposal_key' plus 'fac_ref' (the registered FAC-* in politics.json, or null while unregistered) after p2-merge re-keying. CHAR-* values are forward references (whitelisted) proposed for 03-characters.

_meta.id_policy: No FAC-*/LOC-*/TL-*/SUP-* IDs are referenced as live cross-references in this draft, because politics/geography/timeline/cultivation are being written in parallel and are empty at write time; proposed IDs appear only in 'proposed_*' fields and in cross_domain_assumptions for memory-bible to reconcile at p2-merge.
_meta.locked_by: H1 user signature (G2 PASS), recorded by 00-orchestration/memory-bible task p2-lock
_meta.controlled: Writes only via memory-bible controlled change (WRITE_RULES.md section 5).

setting.era: Mid-Victorian England, a single hot summer afternoon in 1862 (the 4th day of the month; production date July 4, 1862), running from early afternoon on the bank to sunset and tea-time.
setting.place_summary: A grassy bank under trees at the edge of a field in the Thames valley near Oxford, beside a slow river backwater with reeds, with a hedge-line, a working farmyard with sheep and cattle within earshot, and Alice's family house a short run away for tea. Alice, a well-off girl of about ten, dozes there beside her older sister, who is reading. Everything from the White Rabbit to the trial is Alice's dream during that nap; it ends when she wakes with her head in her sister's lap.
setting.scale: Two layers. (1) Waking frame: one riverside meadow, the adjoining farmyard, and the family home, with the wider England Alice knows from lessons and one seaside trip. (2) Dream layer, Wonderland: a small, closed, dream-sized world under the hedge (a hall of doors, a wood, a few houses, the Queen's garden and court, a shore), with one kingdom (Hearts) and a few households. No other nations, no travel between the layers except falling asleep and waking.

setting.reason: The source establishes England (English coast, ch002-p16), summer, a hot afternoon, a bank with trees, a field and a hedge, reeds and a pool, a nearby farmyard (ch012-p70), and a house close enough to run to for tea (ch012-p66). It gives no year, county, river, or age. Designed values: 1862 and Oxford/Thames follow the book's own history (it was first told on a Thames boating trip near Oxford on 4 July 1862, published 1865), which fits every period detail in the text: railway to the seaside, bathing machines, croquet, the schoolroom. The source says 'the fourth' at ch007-p22. 'Riverbank' is a design choice from the reeds and pool, as the work order asks. Age about ten is a world-level working value only; the final age is owned by 03-characters.

period.value: Summer 1862, mid-Victorian England (production date: Friday 4 July 1862). The afternoon runs from about 2 pm to sunset, about 8 pm. Period cues: crinoline-era dress, railway travel to the seaside, the 1860s croquet craze, schoolroom education for girls, and a household run to fixed tea-time.

social_class.value: Comfortable upper-middle-class professional family, the household of a senior clergyman-scholar in a university town. Signs: schoolroom lessons with paid 'extras' (French, music), at least one housemaid, a pet cat fed at tea-time, an older sister free to read on a weekday afternoon, and Alice's pity for a poorer girl's 'poky little house'. Alice was raised to curtsey, recite, and defer to adults. The parents never appear in the source and stay off-screen.

social_class.reason: The class markers are all in the source: schoolroom, French and music, curtsey, tea-time routine, pity for Mabel's poorer home, and knowing what a housemaid is. The father's profession is designed from the book's own history, the Liddell household at Christ Church, Oxford, and is kept generic ('clergyman-scholar'). Individual family members and their names are owned by 03-characters.

riverbank_setting.value: The bank is the story's only waking place: the girl gets bored and drowsy, a real white rabbit dashes past and dives under the hedge, and she falls asleep in the heat. At the end she wakes as leaves fall from the trees, while sheep-bells, a shepherd boy's voice, farmyard clamour, lowing cattle and reeds stirring on the pool carry on around the sister. Light runs from harsh early-afternoon sun to golden sunset.

wonderland_real_counterparts.principle: Wonderland is not a second geography. It is Alice's dream, and its people, places, rules and sounds reshape things from her real day and upbringing: the bank, the rabbit, the hedge, Dinah, the schoolroom, the housemaid, tea-time, croquet, lawcourts read about in books, and the farmyard noises around her sleeping body. The source makes this mapping itself for sounds (ch012-p70) and for the cards (ch012-p64). Everything else below is a design mapping to keep the dream world grounded.
wonderland_real_counterparts.rendering_note: (Added BIB-0027, user ruling 2026-09-22.) The counterparts below ground what the dream is made of, not how it looks on screen. In the dream the talking animals that grow from these real things (the White Rabbit from the real rabbit, the Cheshire Cat from Dinah, and the rest) are photoreal CGI animals in live-action plates (cultivation.json SUP-002, SUP-010, XA-magic-02), and the dream's places that grow from real ones (the garden, the hall, the pool, the court) are dressed in the Art Nouveau painterly design language of WR-010. The waking side of every pair stays plain 1862 realism with ordinary, silent animals.

world_rules.statement: The waking world follows ordinary physics and history: no magic, no talking animals, no size change. Everything impossible happens only inside Alice's dream, and the dream ends when she wakes on the bank.
world_rules.visual_implication: Frame scenes (bank, sister, farm) are shot in plain naturalistic period realism, with ordinary, silent animals only. The dream may bend space and logic with a real camera, real sets and real actors, plus photoreal CGI animal characters and set extensions integrated into the live-action plates (amended BIB-0027, user ruling 2026-09-22; previously 'only in ways a real camera, real sets and real actors can do'). Size changes stay practical and in-camera (XA-03).

source.quote: though she knew she had but to open them again, and all would change to dull reality

also_seen.quote: Oh, I’ve had such a curious dream!

world_rules.reason: The source itself frames Wonderland as a dream. 'No literal magic even inside the dream' follows the premise, and the exact per-element treatment is owned by p2-magic (XA-01).

world_rules.statement: Inside the dream, cause and effect run on dream-logic taken from Alice's waking concerns (lessons, manners, food, time, adult authority). Places may connect impossibly or disappear, but every element must be something a real Victorian child could have seen, heard, read or been taught. One licensed exception (BIB-0027): the look of the dream's environments follows the Art Nouveau design language of WR-010.
world_rules.visual_implication: No fantasy iconography foreign to 1862 England in content: dream sets are built from period things (brick, hedges, pantry shelves, kitchens, lawns, courtrooms), and transitions are dream-cuts, not glowing visual effects. Their surface design (line, ornament, palette, glass) carries the Art Nouveau painterly language of WR-010, realised as photographed physical space (amended BIB-0027; previously 'No fantasy iconography that is foreign to 1862 England').

source.quote: (when she thought it over afterwards, it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this, but at the time it all seemed quite natural)

also_seen.quote: the great hall, with the glass table and the little door, had vanished completely

world_rules.reason: The source's own statement that 'it all seemed quite natural' supports dream-logic. The 'drawn from waking life' limit is a design rule for grounding (see wonderland_real_counterparts).

world_rules.statement: Victorian class and age hierarchy: children defer to adults, girls curtsey and recite, servants are summoned and scolded, and a well-off child looks down on poorer homes. The whole story tests how far Alice will stand up to adult authority.
world_rules.visual_implication: Blocking and eye-lines put adults above the child (standing over, seated on thrones or high stools). Alice's growing 'full size' at the trial shows through posture and framing, and the finale reverses the hierarchy.

source.quote: she tried to curtsey as she spoke

also_seen.quote: that poky little house
she had grown to her full size by this time.

world_rules.statement: Girls of Alice's class are taught at home in a schoolroom: history, geography, arithmetic, recitation, and French and music as extras. Alice's sense of who she is rests on getting these lessons right.
world_rules.visual_implication: Lesson-books, slates and recitation posture (hands folded, standing) are visual shorthand for who Alice is.

world_rules.statement: The household runs on the clock: tea-time is fixed, lateness is a real fault, and the afternoon ends when the sister sends Alice in to tea.
world_rules.visual_implication: Watches, clocks and the light moving from noon to sunset tell the real time. The dream's stopped six o'clock is set against it.

source.quote: now run in to your tea; it’s getting late

also_seen.quote: Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!
her saucer of milk at tea-time

world_rules.statement: The court of justice follows the form of an English trial as a child has read about it: King as judge in a great wig, a jury of twelve, a herald reading the accusation, witnesses, and evidence. In the dream, its procedure is bent by arbitrary royal power ('Sentence first—verdict afterwards').
world_rules.visual_implication: A real 1860s English courtroom (jury-box, raised bench, dock, clerks with slates) staged with period accuracy. The absurdity is in the behaviour, not the set.

source.quote: “That’s the judge,” she said to herself, “because of his great wig.”

also_seen.quote: and those twelve creatures
Nobody moved.

world_rules.statement: In the Kingdom of Hearts, the Queen's death sentences are threats that are never carried out. The adaptation keeps them frightening in the moment but shows no execution, blood or real harm.
world_rules.visual_implication: No on-screen execution, severed heads or blood. The executioner and the soldiers take people into custody only. The fear lives in reaction shots.

source.quote: they never executes nobody, you know

also_seen.quote: all the players, except the King, the Queen, and Alice, were in custody and under sentence of execution

world_rules.statement: Money is British sterling (pounds, shillings, pence, guineas), and the jury does sums in shillings and pence.
world_rules.visual_implication: Only pre-decimal British coins and notes appear. Prices, amounts and ledgers are in £ s d.

source.quote: reduced the answer to shillings and pence

also_seen.quote: it’s worth a hundred pounds!

world_rules.statement: 1862 technology and leisure: railway to the seaside, bathing machines, pocket watches, printed lesson-books, croquet as the fashionable lawn game, and kitchen fires and cauldrons. No later technology.
world_rules.visual_implication: Props, costume and set dressing are limited to 1862 or earlier: no electric light, telephones or motor vehicles. Croquet sets use 1860s mallets and hoops.

source.quote: a row of lodging houses, and behind them a railway station

also_seen.quote: took a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket
Can you play croquet?

world_rules.reason: The items are in the source. The 1862 cut-off follows from setting.era. BIB-0027 note: the H1 1862 lock still holds for props, costume and the whole waking world; only the surface design of dream environments is exempted, by WR-010.

world_rules.statement: The dream's environments are designed in an Art Nouveau painterly language: flowing organic lines, floral and vine ornament, circular halo and roundel motifs, mosaic and stained-glass accents, and a soft pastel-and-gold palette. It is a licensed dream-world anachronism. The waking 1862 frame keeps period plausibility and shows at most a subtle influence of the same language in composition, palette and flora.
world_rules.visual_implication: Dream scenes (the fall, the hall and little door, the pool, the White Rabbit's house, the wood, the Duchess's house, the tea-party, the Queen's garden and croquet-ground, the shore, the court) carry the language fully, realised as photographed physical sets and set extensions in the same live-action plate as the actors and CGI animals: built ironwork, carved wood, glass, mosaic, living and sculpted flora, real light. Never flat poster illustration, outline graphics or a digital matte-painting finish. Costume and hand props stay 1862-based (WR-009) even inside these spaces. Waking scenes (bank, meadow, hedge, farm, family house) use no Art Nouveau ornament; the influence is limited to framing, palette and the wildflowers of the meadow.

source.quote: the loveliest garden you ever saw

world_rules.reason: User ruling in chat, 2026-09-22 (BIB-0027, answer to DEF-p4-style-001 b, extended): add the painting style of Alphonse Mucha to the environments. Scope (dream full, waking subtle, photographed not illustrated) is the workflow-orchestrator's interpretation, to be re-surfaced at H2. The source gives no period-bound look for the dream; the goal-garden quoted above is the image the dream's design grows toward.

tone.genre: Realistic fantasy film adapted from a fairy tale, set in the Victorian period: a coming-of-age story told as a photoreal dream, a child's afternoon nightmare-comedy about identity and adult authority, framed by a sunlit, nostalgic riverbank (amended BIB-0027; previously 'Realistic Victorian period drama and coming-of-age story, told as a grounded dream: ...').
themes: Identity: 'Who in the world am I?' Being told who you are versus deciding it yourself.
Arbitrary adult authority and its nonsense rules, which lose their power once the child stops deferring.
Borrowed schoolroom knowledge breaking down, and the child's own judgment taking over.
Growing up, and the passing of childhood, seen through the older sister's tender reverie.

source.quote: Who in the world am I? Ah, _that’s_ the great puzzle!

also_seen.quote: Who cares for you?
remembering her own child-life, and the happy summer days

tone.reason: The themes are in the source (story_graph summary: 'who am I / whose authority counts'). The genre label is set by brief.md, 'Realistic fantasy film adapted from a fairy tale' (quote corrected at BIB-0027), and by the user's 2026-09-22 ruling that the film is realistic fantasy.

history_overview.summary: The Norman Conquest: William the Conqueror takes England; the earls Edwin and Morcar of Mercia and Northumbria submit. This is the only real history the source quotes, and it appears as dry schoolroom text that the Mouse recites.

source.quote: Edwin and Morcar, the earls of Mercia and Northumbria

history_overview.summary: Alice has been raised and taught in the schoolroom, has been to the English seaside once by railway, knows other girls of her age (Ada, Mabel) and a neighbour farmer's terrier, and has a cat, Dinah.

source.quote: Alice had been to the seaside once in her life

history_overview.summary: Last March, at the Queen of Hearts' great concert, the Hatter quarrelled with Time, and it has been six o'clock ever since. Earlier still, the Mock Turtle and the Gryphon went to school in the sea. The Queen made the tarts 'all on a summer day', and the Knave is accused of stealing them.

source.quote: We quarrelled last March—just before _he_ went mad, you know—

also_seen.quote: The Queen of Hearts, she made some tarts, All on a summer day

history_overview.summary: On the bank, Alice falls asleep and dreams Wonderland. The dream's power structure runs from scattered hosts (the pool, the Rabbit's house, the wood, the Duchess, the tea-party) to the centralised terror of the Hearts court (croquet, then the trial). Its authority collapses when Alice defies it at full size, and she wakes.

source.quote: and found herself lying on the bank

history_overview.period: The after-time (the sister's vision of the future)
history_overview.summary: The sister imagines Alice grown into a woman who keeps her childlike heart and tells children the dream of Wonderland.

source.quote: be herself a grown woman

open_questions.question: How is each impossible element of the dream rendered on screen (talking animals and cards, size changes, transformations, the fall)? The world layer assumes a grounded dream played by human actors; see XA-01 to XA-04.
open_questions.resolution: Resolved: the user approved SUP-001 to SUP-014 as written at the H1 pre-ruling (5.1 A, runs/h1-ruling/ruling.json (user, 2026-09-22T17:33:21+08:00)). The dream frame is explicit; dream-figures are human performers; size and space effects are practical and in-camera; Time is a metaphor; threats are never enacted. AMENDED by user ruling 2026-09-22 (BIB-0027): talking animals, the Gryphon and the Mock Turtle are photoreal CGI animals/creatures in live-action plates (SUP-002, SUP-010); card figures and human dream-figures stay human performers (SUP-004); dream environments carry the Art Nouveau design language of WR-010. Everything else in this resolution stands.

source.quote: Oh, I’ve had such a curious dream!

open_questions.question: Alice's age, family surname and the names of her sister and parents.
open_questions.resolution: The source never reveals them. Working values confirmed at the H1 pre-ruling (5.6 A): Alice about ten, her sister in her mid-teens, parents off-screen. Names and final ages are owned by 03-characters.

source.quote: very few little girls of her age knew the meaning of it at all

open_questions.question: The trial's verdict and the Knave's guilt.
open_questions.resolution: The source never reveals them: Alice wakes before any verdict (ev0052 to ev0053). Production value: no verdict, the scene cuts on the cards flying up.

source.quote: Sentence first—verdict afterwards.

open_questions.question: Whether the Cheshire Cat's 'execution' and the Duchess's sentence were ever settled.
open_questions.resolution: The source never reveals it (events.json broken_chains ev0038 and ev0039; story_graph fs-021). Production value: no one is executed (WR-007), and the Duchess simply does not appear after ch009.

source.quote: She’s under sentence of execution.

open_questions.question: Where exactly the bank is, and which river.
open_questions.resolution: The source gives only the bank, field, hedge, trees, pool and reeds. Resolved by design as a Thames backwater meadow near Oxford (setting, frame.place). Fine layout is owned by 02-worldbuilding/geography.

source.quote: the pool rippling to the waving of the reeds
